record.description: Chrysippus distinguished between perfect and principal causes (causae perfectae et principales) and auxiliary/proximate causes (causae adiuvantes et proximae). An external impression (phantasia) is only an auxiliary cause of assent; the principal cause is the agent's own character (the cylinder's shape). This distinction allowed Chrysippus to maintain both universal causal determinism and moral responsibility: actions are necessitated only by auxiliary causes, while their principal cause remains the agent's own nature. Reported by Cicero, De Fato 41-43; also Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae VII.2.
record.label: Chrysippus's Causal Taxonomy (Causes Perfect/Auxiliary)

conclusion.text: Chrysippus's causal taxonomy reconciles universal causal determinism with moral responsibility by locating the principal cause of action in the agent's own nature, while relegating external impressions to the status of auxiliary causes that merely trigger or occasion assent without determining its specific qualitative character.

premises.text: There exists a distinction between perfect and principal causes (causae perfectae et principales) and auxiliary/proximate causes (causae adiuvantes et proximae) in Stoic causal analysis.
An external impression (phantasia) is an auxiliary/proximate cause of assent, not a perfect/principal cause.
The agent's own character or nature (analogized to the cylinder's shape) is the perfect/principal cause of assent and subsequent action.
Universal causal determinism (fatum) obtains: every event has a cause, and causes are themselves caused in an unbroken chain.

An action is 'necessitated' in the sense of being triggered or occasioned by auxiliary causes, but the qualitative determination of the action (its specific character as this or that action) derives from the principal cause.
Moral responsibility (to eph' hēmin) requires that the agent be the principal cause of the action, not merely that the action be uncaused or contingent upon external circumstances.

validity_assessment.rationale: The argument is formally valid if one grants the Stoic causal framework and the identification of moral responsibility with principal causation. However, scholarly acceptance is disputed: critics (beginning with ancient opponents, e.g., Carneades via Cicero) argue that if auxiliary causes necessitate the occasion of assent and principal causes are themselves antecedently determined, the agent's 'own nature' is not ultimately up to the agent. The 'reconciliation' depends on a compatibilist premise (P6) that many scholars and ancient critics reject as question-begging. Bobzien (1998) argues Chrysippus achieves a coherent compatibilism; others (e.g., Salles 2005, Barnes 1983) dispute whether principal/auxiliary causation successfully preserves anything recognizable as moral responsibility against incompatibilist challenge.

metadata.verified_reference: Cicero, De Fato 41–43 (causarum aliae perfectae et principales, aliae adiuvantes et proximae; cylinder/cone analogy); Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae VII.2 (Chrysippus on fate + cylinder). Both loci accurate; Latin terms are Cicero's verbatim wording.

record.description: The Cylinder Analogy is Chrysippus' most famous argument defending what modern scholars term Stoic compatibilism. Imagine a cylinder on a hill: when pushed, it rolls down. Why does it roll? Two causes: (1) External: the push that initiates motion; (2) Internal: the cylindrical shape that determines rolling vs. sliding. Similarly, human action has: (1) External causes: impressions (φαντασίαι) presented to us by fate; (2) Internal causes: our character, reason, and assent (συγκατάθεσις). Moral responsibility attaches to internal causes. Just as the cylinder's rolling is explained by its shape (not just the push), our actions are explained by our character (not just external impressions). The key move: even though both push and shape are fated, we don't blame the push for the cylinder's rolling - we 'blame' its cylindrical nature. Likewise, even though character is fated, responsibility attaches to character, not external causes. Critics (especially Alexander) objected: This doesn't save freedom! If the cylinder's nature is itself determined by prior causes, the cylinder isn't a true originator. Chrysippus conflates two questions: (1) Where is the proximate cause? (Answer: internal character); (2) Is the agent an undetermined originator? (Answer: no, under fate). The analogy only addresses (1), leaving (2) - the freedom question - unanswered.
record.label: Cylinder Analogy (Internal vs. External Causation)

ancient_sources: Cicero, De Fato 42-43 - Full exposition of cylinder and cone analogy: external push (antecedent cause) vs. shape/nature (perfect and principal cause)
Gellius, Noctes Atticae 7.2.6-14 - Cylinder analogy: impressions (visum) do not necessitate assent; agent's nature (natura animi, dispositio) is decisive
Gellius, Noctes Atticae 7.2.9-11 - Distinction between antecedent causes (causae antecedentes) and perfect/principal causes (causae perfectae et principales)
Alexander of Aphrodisias, De Fato 181.13-182.20 - Critical discussion of Chrysippean cylinder analogy
metadata.bobzien_2001_judgement: Bobzien 2001 §6.3.3 (p. 258-271) supplies the definitive modern reconstruction of Chrysippus's cylinder-and-cone analogy. Key moves: (a) the cylinder's roll is determined by the push (antecedent cause) + its own shape (internal nature); (b) moral responsibility attaches to the internal nature, not the push; (c) the analogy is a model of compatibilist causation, not of libertarian freedom. Sources = Cic. Fat. 39-44 + Gellius NA 7.2

conclusion.text: Human moral responsibility is preserved within Stoic determinism (fate) through the distinction between external initiating causes and internal principal causes, even though the agent is not an undetermined originator of action.

premises.text: External impressions (phantasiai) present themselves to the human soul, initiating but not completing the process of assent.

Just as a cylinder cannot begin to move unless pushed, but the push gives it only the beginning of motion and not its rollability (volubilitas), so too the external impression impresses itself upon the mind but does not give assent.
Assent (synkatathesis) is 'in our power' (in potestate nostra) in the sense that its completion depends upon our internal nature, character, and reason.

Moral responsibility (to eph' hēmin) attaches to the internal cause (character/assent) rather than the external cause (impression), just as we attribute the cylinder's rolling to its shape rather than to the push.
The internal cause (character/assent) is itself fated and determined by prior causes, yet this does not eliminate the distinction between proximate cause (internal) and initiating cause (external).

For Stoic causal analysis, the principal cause (aition) of an action is the agent's character and assent, while external impressions function as proximate/auxiliary causes (sunaitia/prokatarktika); this distinction is sufficient for the Stoic account of responsibility.

validity_assessment.rationale: The argument is formally valid as a conditional chain: if responsibility requires only distinction between internal/external causes (P1-P4), and if internal causes are principal causes (P6), then responsibility is preserved (C). However, scholarly acceptance is deeply disputed: Alexander of Aphrodisias and later critics argue that the argument commits a modal fallacy—conflating (a) 'assent is in our power' in the sense of being internally caused, with (b) 'assent is in our power' in the sense of being open to alternative possibilities. The cylinder analogy only establishes (a), leaving the compatibilist conclusion question-begging against incompatibilist critics. See Bobzien 1998, ch. 6, on the distinction between proximate and principal causes in Stoic theory.
validity_assessment.scholarly_consensus: The argument is widely regarded as Chrysippus's central compatibilist move, but whether it successfully answers the 'freedom question' (as opposed to merely the 'causal location' question) remains contested. The attestation of P4-P6 as 'reconstructed' reflects that Chrysippus likely did not distinguish these as separate argumentative steps; the modern scholarly reconstruction (especially Bobzien 1998; also Salles 2005) separates the causal analysis from the normative conclusion that critics like Alexander challenged.

record.description: Stoic analogy (attributed to Zeno and Chrysippus by Hippolytus, Refutatio 1.21) illustrating acceptance of fate. A dog tied to a moving cart will be pulled along whether it wants to follow or not; it can either resist and be dragged, or run alongside willingly. Similarly, humans are bound to fate but can choose their attitude: the wise person wills what happens, while the fool is dragged reluctantly. Shows that freedom consists in willing alignment with fate, not in having alternative possibilities.
record.label: The Dog and Cart Argument

ancient_sources: Epictetus, Discourses (implied analogy; not explicitly stated but consistent with I.1, II.2)

conclusion.text: Human freedom is constituted by the internal disposition of assent (sunkatathesis) aligned with necessitated external events, not by causal indeterminacy or the power to do otherwise.

legacy_premises: A dog is tied to a moving cart
If the dog follows willingly, it is pulled and follows (voluntary)
If the dog does not follow willingly, it is dragged by force (involuntary)
In either case, the dog ends up following the cart (outcome is fated)
We can either assent willingly (virtue) or be dragged unwillingly (vice)

premises.text: A dog tied to a moving cart is compelled to follow the cart's motion regardless of its own volition.
If the dog follows willingly, it moves alongside the cart in a manner that preserves its own agency (voluntary motion).
If the dog does not follow willingly, it is dragged by force in a manner that violates its own agency (involuntary motion).
In either case, the dog necessarily follows the cart; the outcome is not subject to the dog's choice.
Humans stand in an analogous relation to fate (heimarmenē) as the dog stands to the cart: external events are necessitated and not 'up to us' (ouk eph' hēmin).
The locus of what is 'up to us' (eph' hēmin) in humans is restricted to judgment (dogma), assent (sunkatathesis), and impulse (hormē) directed toward presented impressions (phantasiai).
The wise person (spoudaios) assents to fate willingly, aligning his hormē with the course of events; this constitutes virtue and the good (agathon).
The fool (phaulos) resists fate with negative dogmata, experiencing his necessitated motion as drag (helkesthai); this constitutes vice (kakia).
Freedom (eleutheria) consists in willing alignment with fate, not in the possession of alternative possibilities (to dynaton houtō kai houtō).

validity_assessment.rationale: The argument proceeds by analogy (parabolē), not strict syllogistic form. The inference from canine behavior to human psychology is analogical, not deductive. The Stoics treat the dog-cart as an illustration (endeigma) rather than a proof (apodeixis). The gap between 'is dragged' and 'experiences being dragged' requires the additional Stoic premise that value-judgments (axiai) determine affective state (pathos), which is not supplied in the Hippolytan report. The argument is formally valid only if supplemented by Stoic axiology; as reported, it commits the fallacy of false analogy unless one already accepts Stoic moral psychology. Scholarly acceptance of the argument's validity is disputed: Bobzien (1998, ch. 6) distinguishes proximate cause (the dog's own hormē as auxiliary cause, sunaition) from principal cause (the cart/fate as primary cause, aition), noting that the analogy obscures the complexity of human sunkatathesis; Salles (2005) defends the argument's coherence within Stoic compatibilism; while Sorabji (1980) and Frede (2011) question whether this constitutes 'freedom' in any recognizable sense. The theological loading of autexousion in later Patristic reception (e.g., Origen, Clement) introduces further divergence from the original Stoic framework.
validity_assessment.scholarly_consensus: The argument is accepted as authentically Stoic (Zeno/Chrysippus via Hippolytus, Ref. 1.21 = SVF 2.975) but disputed as to its philosophical adequacy. The doxographical attestation is secure; the reconstruction of P7-P9 requires supplementation from Epictetan and Chrysippean material (see Bobzien 1998; Inwood 1985; Long & Sedley 1987, 62A-B).

record.description: Diodorus Cronus' (fl. 4th c. BCE, Megarian school) famous argument about possibility and necessity, preserved in Epictetus (Diss. 2.19). The argument uses three premises to conclude that only what is or will be is possible, effectively collapsing modal distinctions and supporting determinism. Diodorus accepted: (1) Every past truth is necessary, (2) The impossible does not follow from the possible, and rejected (3) Something is possible which neither is nor will be true.
record.label: The Master Argument (Kurieuon Logos)

ancient_sources: Alexander of Aphrodisias, In Analytica Priora 177-184
metadata.bobzien_2001_judgement: Bobzien 2001 §3.1.2 reconstructs the Master Argument as Diodorus Cronus's argument for necessitarianism: from (1) every past truth is necessary, (2) the impossible does not follow from the possible, infer (3) every possible is or will be true. This collapses possible-but-not-actual into the impossible. Chrysippus's modal system is explicitly designed to escape this collapse
metadata.conclusion: These three propositions form an inconsistent triad. Diodorus rejected (3), concluding that only what is or will be actual is possible.

record.description:
**Étymologie** : *clinamen* < lat. *clinare* (« incliner, pencher »), néologisme lucrétien (DRN II.292) calque du grec παρέγκλισις (Épicure, ap. Aetius I.12.5, I.23.4 ; Diogène d'Œnoanda fr. 54) ; *parenklisis* < παρά- + ἐγκλίνω.

The clinamen or atomic swerve is the Epicurean doctrine that atoms spontaneously deviate minutely from their downward trajectories 'at no fixed place or time' (Lucretius: incerto tempore... incertisque locis). This uncaused, indeterministic motion at the atomic level breaks the chain of deterministic causation inherited from Democritus' mechanistic atomism. Without the swerve, all atomic motions would be strictly determined by prior causes stretching back infinitely, leaving no room for autonomous action or free will. The swerve is described as minimal (exiguum clinamen) - the smallest possible deviation - yet its effects cascade upward from atomic to psychological and moral levels. Epicurus introduced the swerve explicitly to ground human freedom and moral responsibility: if everything were determined, praise, blame, and deliberation would be pointless. The doctrine is not preserved in any of Epicurus' three surviving letters; it is reported in the doxography (Diogenes Laertius X) and in Stoic/Academic critics (Cicero, De Fato 22-23, 46-48), and developed most fully in Lucretius, De Rerum Natura II.216-293. Ancient critics (Cicero, Stoics) attacked it as ad hoc and scientifically baseless - an uncaused motion invoked merely to save ethics. Modern interpreters debate whether the swerve operates at the moment of human choice or merely breaks determinism in the causal background. The clinamen represents the first systematic philosophical appeal to indeterminism to ground free will - a move that would recur in modern quantum indeterminacy theories.
record.label: Clinamen / Parenklisis (Atomic Swerve)

modern_scholarship: Furley, David J. Two Studies in the Greek Atomists, Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1967, Study II “Aristotle and Epicurus on Voluntary Action” — the classic argument that the swerve is NOT the direct cause of individual volitions but blocks the inheritance of character by ancestral atomic motion.

Bobzien, Susanne. “Did Epicurus Discover the Free Will Problem?”, Oxford Studies in Ancient Philosophy 19 (2000), 287-337 — the strongest deflationary case: no surviving evidence that Epicurus grounded moral responsibility on a freedom to do otherwise; action is determined by the agent's developed mental disposition.
metadata.source_provenance_caveat: PROVENANCE CAVEAT (2026-08-03): the formulation “Epicurus introduced the swerve in order to preserve freedom” is nowhere in a surviving text of Epicurus himself. It rests on (a) Lucretius, DRN II.251-293, and (b) the hostile Ciceronian testimony at De fato 22-23 and De natura deorum I.69-70. On Nature XXV (PHerc. 697/1191) discusses responsibility and the developed self without invoking the swerve. Attribute the thesis to its ancient witnesses and its modern proponents (Fowler 1983, Englert 1987, Purinton 1999), never to a scholar who does not defend it.

Greek παρέγκλισις attested in the doxography (Aetius I.12.5, I.23.4) and Diogenes of Oenoanda, NOT in Diogenes Laertius X.

record.description:
**Termes** : κύλινδρος (kylindros) ; lat. cylindrus (Cic., *De Fato* 42) ; l'analogie chrysippéenne du cylindre pour la causalité interne.

Chrysippus' famous analogy to explain how external causes (fate) and internal nature (character) jointly determine action without eliminating moral responsibility. The Analogy: Just as when you push a cylinder, the push (external cause) starts the motion but the rolling (effect) happens "according to its own nature" (cylindrical shape), so too when an impression strikes the mind, the impression (external cause) prompts the response but the assent (effect) happens according to the mind's own nature (character/dispositions). Philosophical point: The external antecedent cause (impression) is auxiliary/proximate (adiuvans et proxima), NOT perfect/principal (perfecta et principalis). The mind's nature is the principal cause. Therefore assent is: (1) fated (fully determined) but (2) NOT necessary (not externally forced). We are responsible because WE (our nature) are the principal cause. Sources: Cicero, De Fato 42-43; Gellius, NA 7.2.11 (Bobzien 2001, pp. 268-275).
record.label: Cylinder Analogy (Chrysippus)

record.description:
**Étymologie** : τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, syntagme attributif « ce qui est sur nous / en notre pouvoir » < ἐπί + datif pronom personnel 1ʳᵉ pl. Locution technique aristotélicienne (*EN* III.5) reprise par les Stoïciens et les Médio-Platoniciens.

To eph' hêmin (τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, what is in our power/up to us) is Aristotle's concept for the domain of human agency and responsibility - actions and states that genuinely depend on us and are therefore proper objects of praise and blame. In Nicomachean Ethics III.5, Aristotle argues that virtue and vice are eph' hêmin because the actions that form our character are in our power: 'where acting is up to us, so is not acting' (1113b6-7). We deliberate about and choose among alternatives that are 'in our power' (ἐφ' ἡμῖν). The concept implies: (1) genuine alternatives - we can do otherwise, (2) internal origin - the source is in us, (3) rational control - we deliberate and choose. Aristotle connects this to voluntary action and deliberate choice: what is eph' hêmin is voluntary (hekousion) and the proper domain of prohairesis. The concept became absolutely central to ancient debates about freedom and fate. The Stoics accepted that actions are eph' hêmin in the sense of 'in our power' but claimed this is compatible with fate - the action's origin is in us even though it's causally necessitated. Alexander of Aphrodisias argued that genuine 'up to us' requires two-way power to do otherwise, incompatible with determinism (a position now widely characterized as libertarian). Carneades used the concept in anti-fatalist arguments: if fate holds, nothing is truly eph' hêmin, destroying moral agency. Bobzien's Critical Distinction (1998): Susanne Bobzien identifies two fundamentally different concepts historically conflated under ἐφ' ἡμῖν: (1) One-sided causative (Stoic): 'If X is eph' hêmin, not-X is NOT eph' hêmin' - expresses causal attribution, compatible with determinism. (2) Two-sided potestative (Peripatetic/Platonist): 'If X is eph' hêmin, not-X is also eph' hêmin' - expresses power for alternatives. Aristotle used two-sided eph' hêmin but was not an indeterminist. Middle-Platonists synthesized Aristotelian texts ambiguously. Alexander of Aphrodisias (late 2nd c. CE) is often credited with being the first to make two-sided eph' hêmin explicitly indeterminist, thus inaugurating the modern free-will problem. The ancient debates often talked past each other due to this conceptual ambiguity.
record.label: To Eph' Hêmin (Τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν) - What is In Our Power

metadata.destree2014_collective_thesis: Le eph' hêmin commence sa vie philosophique chez Aristote (Ch. 3-6), est technique chez Chrysippe (controverse Gourinat ch. 9), devient causal chez Épictète (Salles ch. 11), critique du libertarianisme moderne (Sauvé Meyer ch. 5 anti-PAP). Le libre arbitre n'émerge qu'à l'antiquité tardive (Frede M. ch. 22 + Wildberg ch. 21 + Horn ch. 19)
metadata.destree2014_treatment: Concept-pivot de tout le volume Destrée 2014 — 20 chapitres convergeant sur l'analyse historique-conceptuelle du eph' hêmin
metadata.frede_2011_treatment: Frede 2011 — to eph' hēmin is the spine of the whole narrative. In Aristotle (Ch. 2, p. 27) it picks out actions whose getting-done depends entirely on us (the precondition for choice). In classical Stoicism (Ch. 5, p. 75) it covers any action depending on our assent. In Epictetus (Ch. 5, p. 75-76) it is sharply narrowed : not the external action but only the assent to the impulsive impression — this is the conceptual move that makes a free will articulable. In Alexander (Ch. 6, p. 96-100) it requires more than unforced assent : critical rational evaluation. In Origen (Ch. 7, p. 112) eph' hēmin is identified with autexousion. In Augustine (Ch. 9, p. 168) liberum arbitrium = eph' hēmin in the Stoic sense, retained even after the loss of libertas

metadata.furst_2022_key_thesis: Fürst 2022 (suivant Bobzien Determinism and Freedom 280 Anm. 95) : la forme substantivée τὸ ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν n'est pas attestée pour le Vieux-Stoïcisme et ne peut au plus tôt se trouver derrière les formulations latines in nostra potestate ou sita in nobis. Le rendu fréquent par « volonté » ou « liberté » ou « liberté de la volonté » est « franchement trompeur » selon Fürst — il s'agit de « ce qui dépend de nous », non de la volonté

record.description: The ancient Stoics — above all Chrysippus (c. 279–c. 206 BCE) — faced a central challenge: how to maintain that everything occurs according to heimarmene (εἱμαρμένη), an eternal and unbreakable causal chain governed by divine Logos, while preserving a meaningful domain of human agency, to eph' hemin (τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, what is up to us), sufficient for moral praise and blame. Modern scholars, beginning especially with Bobzien (1998) and Sharples (1986), characterize the resulting Stoic position as a form of "compatibilism," though this label is anachronistic and debated. Chrysippus's strategy rested on several interlocking moves. First, a causal taxonomy: he distinguished proximate/auxiliary causes (causae adiuvantes et proximae) from perfect/principal causes (causae perfectae et principales). An external impression (phantasia) merely initiates action, but the principal cause is the agent's own character — just as a push sets a cylinder rolling, but the cylinder's shape determines how it rolls (Cicero, De Fato 42–43). Second, synkatathesis (συγκατάθεσις, assent): the rational soul's assent to an impression is determined by character yet remains the agent's own act, grounding responsibility within the causal order rather than outside it. Third, confatalia (συμπεπλεγμένα, co-fated events): against the Lazy Argument (argos logos), which held that if outcomes are fated then effort is pointless, Chrysippus argued that outcomes and their means are fated together — recovery is co-fated with consulting a doctor (Cicero, De Fato 28–30). Critically, the Stoic conception of eph' hemin is one-sided and causative: that x depends on us does not entail that not-x also depends on us, unlike Aristotle's two-sided, potestative reading (EN III.5, 1113b7–8). Alexander of Aphrodisias (De Fato 9–15, 33–38) mounted the most sustained ancient critique, arguing that this one-sided notion collapses genuine agency into mere causal origination, and that Chrysippus's cylinder analogy ultimately fails to distinguish a morally responsible agent from a determined natural process.
record.label: Stoic Compatibilism and Moral Responsibility

metadata.key_question: How did Stoics reconcile determinism with moral responsibility?

record.description: Aristotle on causation and necessity — Aristotle separates necessity from causation: actions open to moral scrutiny may be caused without being necessitated. Sorabji reads Aristotle as an indeterminist about human action as well as about coincidences: in the very same circumstances the agent could have acted otherwise. What he denies Aristotle is not undetermined agency but the libertarian machinery usually attached to it — 'fresh starts', uncaused causes and a faculty of will; on his reading no break in the causal chain is required, because causes are primarily explanatory rather than necessitating.
record.label: Aristotle on causation and necessity

attested_by: Sorabji, *Necessity, Cause and Blame* (1980), pp. xi, 26, 139, 229, 232, 242, 250.

conclusion.text: Aristotle's theory of causation is indeterminist with respect to chance events and separates causal explanation from necessitation, but this does not amount to a libertarian doctrine of human agency; rather, human actions are caused by deliberative choice without being causally necessitated, and causes function primarily as explanations rather than as necessitating physical determinants.

metadata.dialectical_repairs_2026_08_17_claim_fix: The node said Sorabji denies Aristotle a doctrine of libertarian human agency. He affirms undetermined human action and denies only the uncaused-cause apparatus. Sorabji 1980, p. 139: 'In Chapter Fourteen, I shall further deny that Aristotle's account of action is deterministic'; p. 242: 'my case against deterministic interpretations, by denying that Aristotle's treatment of action is wholly deterministic… Aristotle is an indeterminist in the sense defined in the Introduction, but not in the more radical sense suggested by others'; p. 232 n. 9: 'In the very same circumstances, the child could have acted in the other way.' The 'fresh starts' he rejects are Ross's, Furley's and Hardie's (pp. 26 n. 1, 229). He never uses 'free will' in his own voice.

premises.text: Aristotle distinguishes between necessity (anankē) and causation (aitia), such that a cause may explain why something comes about without necessitating that it must come about.
Actions subject to moral scrutiny (ta prakta) are caused by the agent's deliberation and choice, yet remain 'up to us' (eph' hēmin) and not necessitated.

Aristotle's account of chance (tuchē) and spontaneity (to automaton) in Physics II.4-6 treats these as genuine causes that operate without deterministic necessity, indicating indeterminism about certain causal processes.
Aristotle does not hold a doctrine of libertarian free will in the modern sense: the agent's causation of action does not require the will to be an uncaused cause or to possess contra-causal freedom.
For Aristotle, causes (aitiai) are primarily explanatory—answering the 'why' (dia ti)—rather than productive factors that necessitate their effects by physical compulsion.

metadata.stance: Aristotle separates necessity from causation: actions open to moral scrutiny may be caused without being necessitated. Aristotle was an indeterminist about chance, but did not have a doctrine of libertarian human agency. Causes are primarily explanatory rather than necessitating.

validity_assessment.rationale: The argument moves from distinct textual domains (chance, moral action, causal explanation) to a unified interpretive conclusion about Aristotle's position. The inference from 'causes need not necessitate' and 'chance is indeterminist' to 'Aristotle is an indeterminist about causation but not a libertarian' is a scholarly synthesis rather than a formally valid deduction. The suppressed premise—that indeterminism about chance plus non-necessitating causes in ethics jointly constitute a general 'indeterminist' position—is interpretively contested. Sorabji's reading is disputed by compatibilist interpreters (e.g., Meyer 1993, Everson 1990) who argue that eph' hēmin is compatible with causal determinism. The formal gap between 'not necessitated' and 'indeterminist' is precisely the locus of scholarly controversy.

changed_non_quote_fields.eight_context: NEW FINDING. Sorabji enumerates EIGHT distinct Stoic strategies (first two = reply to Diodorus' Master Argument; third = Cicero De Fato VI.12-VII.14 on alternative possibilities; fourth = Cicero De Fato VII.15-16; fifth = Philonian definition of possibility; sixth = epistemic possibility; seventh = Carneades' uncaused motions; eighth = denial that 'caused' entails 'necessitated'). The famous dog-and-cart simile (SVF II) is presented verbatim. Essential anchor for any KG node on Stoic causation/fate vocabulary or for the Carneades response.
